title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme
content: Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme. The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so. British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc. On Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister , Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public. Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off. But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans. One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.” A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.” Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry. In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”. Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota. The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers. British access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles. EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks. The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases. Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states. Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures. Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months . But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”. Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses. Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”. Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course. UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme. The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs. This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels. The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements. The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.

final_quality.reason: This article reports a significant development in the UK's relationship with the EU, specifically the potential for discounted university fees for EU students in exchange for access to the EU's industrial programme. The article provides concrete numbers (£450m a year) and quotes from knowledgeable sources, making it a substantive and important piece for readers interested in UK-EU relations and education.

title: Ukraine air raid app apparently hacked as users receive false radiation threat, Air Force says
content:
Ukraine's air raid alert app was apparently hacked on Sunday and for a short time said the capital Kyiv was subject to a radiation threat, the Ukrainian Air Force has said.
The alert on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
The Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation on the threat of air strikes.
A few hours later Russian authorities said its app was hacked. A Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Russia has the world's biggest nuclear arsenal, and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly suggested an openness to using all weapons at Russia's disposal .
The alerts, in Ukrainian, started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT), with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide. Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat.  Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying".
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49, a fourth alert stated there was a "Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
In a separate post on Telegram, the Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said that due to the Air Alert application, the Radiation Hazard signal was played on loudspeaker devices in the Lviv region, and added there was no threat of radiation hazard.
If the alert app is not working, Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation advises the public to turn on notifications on their smartphones, pay attention to sirens, and to only read official sources
Several leaders of other regions also posted on Telegram that the app had apparently been hacked and there was no local threat.
"Everything is calm in the region for now," said Svitlana Onyshchuk, the governor of the Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. The app had reported a red-level air raid alert for the oblast in Ukraine's east, between 22:50 and 23:57.
The Vinnytsia regional head, Natalya Zabolotna, said there had been a cyber-attack on the Air Alert app and posted a warning on Telegram not to click on the link in the message, which could be a phishing attempt.
The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry had earlier said the app was temporarily disabled for maintenance after it had "apparently been compromised". It urged residents to turn on their smartphones' emergency notifications so they could receive state-issued distress signals.
A few hours after the false alerts in Ukraine, Russia's ministry of emergency situations said its app had been subjected to "a massive cyberattack" which sent "fake information to the public".
No further details were given by the ministry or state media.
Ukrainian news outlet, UNN, reported the hack sent fake alerts of a nuclear threat inside Russia.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian held territory, said on its Telegram page that the app had been hacked, accompanied with laughing emojis.
ranking_reason: Air raid app hack in Ukraine, impacting national security and public awareness

analysis.reason: Air raid app hack in Ukraine, impacting national security and public awareness

final_quality.reason: Reports of a national security threat, such as a radiation alert, can be a significant development, and this article provides evidence-based information about the hack and subsequent warnings. The fact that the hack affected a national air raid alert system, and potentially caused panic and disruption, makes this story newsworthy and worthy of publication.

title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
content:
A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.
The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.
On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.
The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.
In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.
Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.
Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".
He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo.
It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was expanded across the wider region of Kherson.
Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack.
Residents trapped there were suffering severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The truce allowed for Oleskhy residents to evacuate if they wanted, and there were emotional scenes on Saturday of reunions between loved ones who hadn't seen eachother for years.
There are Ukrainian military positions just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.

final_quality.reason: The article provides a clear and concise overview of the current situation in Ukraine, reporting on Russian strikes and their impact on the country's energy infrastructure and civilians. It also includes quotes from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, providing context and insight into the situation. The article is a substantive and important development in the category of conflict and war, and provides a clear reason for readers to care.
